judges of the Court of Criminal Appeals have no power to render a 
final decision on behalf of the United States unless permitted to do so 
by other executive officers.
520 U.S. at 664-65.
The case thus gave Justice Scaha an opportunity to somewhat marginalize 
Morrison and its rehance on balancing to decide on what counts as 
constitutional “inferiority.” Officers are inferior, according to the Court, if their 
“work is directed and supervised at some level by others who were appointed 
by presidential nomination with the advice and consent of the Senate.” 520
U. S. at 663. It is not clear, however, whether Morrison-type balancing would 
have dictated a different result. The jurisdiction of the judges at issue in 
Edmond was broader than that of independent counsel, but their control by 
superior officers was much greater. Of course, the very unpredictability of a 
balancing outcome was a core reason for Justice Scalia’s preference for a 
bright-line rule in this context (and in virtually all others). Note that, in relying 
heavily on Edmond, the Arthrex Court also repeats Edmond's caution: “[W]e 
do not attempt to ‘set forth an exclusive criterion for distinguishing between 
principal and inferior officers for Appointments Clause purposes.’ ”
2. 
Interbranch Appointments. Because the statute at issue in Morrison
V. Olson entailed the judicial appointment of a criminal prosecutor, the Court 
also confronted an argument that such a judicial role violated the separation 
of powers. The Court disagreed:
Appellees argue that even if appellant is an “inferior” officer, the 
Clause does not empower Congress to place the power to appoint such 
an officer outside the Executive Branch. They contend that the 
Clause does not contemplate congressional authorization of 
“interbranch appointments,” in which an officer of one branch is 
appointed by officers of another branch. * * * On its face, the 
language of this “excepting clause” admits of no limitation on 
interbranch appointments. Indeed, the inclusion of “as they think 
proper” seems clearly to give Congress significant discretion to 
determine whether it is “proper” to vest the appointment of, for 
example, executive officials in the “courts of Law.” We recognized as 
much in one of our few decisions in this area. Ex parte Siehold, [100 
U.S. (10 Otto) 371, 397—98 (1879)], where we stated:
It is no doubt usual and proper to vest the appointment of 
inferior officers in that department of the government, executive 
or judicial, or in that particular executive department to which 
the duties of such officers appertain. But there is no absolute 
requirement to this effect in the Constitution; and, if there were, 
it would be difficult in many cases to d ft termine to which 
department an office properly belonged. * * *
